The must-sees

  • British Museum

    Museum · 1759

    Founded in 1753 from Hans Sloane’s collection. The Great Court and the round Reading Room sit under a glass roof added in 2000.

    Look for: Find the Rosetta Stone: one decree written in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, the key that unlocked Egyptian writing.

  • Buckingham Palace

    Palace · 1703

    George III bought Buckingham House as a private home, and it became the official palace under Victoria. Royal public appearances are made from its front balcony.

    Look for: Check the flag on the roof: the Royal Standard means the monarch is in, the Union Flag means they are not.

  • Houses of Parliament

    Civic building · 1870

    A fire in 1834 destroyed most of the medieval palace, and Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin rebuilt it in Gothic Revival style. Big Ben is the bell; the tower is the Elizabeth Tower.

    Look for: Look to the top of the Elizabeth Tower: a lamp there is lit whenever either House is sitting after dark.

  • National Gallery

    Museum · 1838

    Founded in 1824 so the public could see a national collection. The building on the square opened in 1838.

    Look for: Look down in the entrance hall: Boris Anrep’s floor mosaics show public figures of his day, Churchill among them, as virtues.

  • St Paul’s Cathedral

    Church · 1710

    The medieval cathedral burned in the Great Fire of 1666, and Christopher Wren’s new church was completed in 1710. Its dome became a symbol of survival through the Blitz.

    Look for: In the crypt, beside Wren’s plain tomb, a Latin inscription reads: if you seek his monument, look around.

  • Tower Bridge

    Building · 1894

    Finished in 1894, it is a bascule bridge dressed as a Gothic castle. The high walkways were built so people could cross while the road was raised.

    Look for: The Gothic stone of the towers is cladding over a steel frame, added so the bridge would suit the Tower beside it.

  • Tower of London

    Fortress · 1078

    The White Tower went up in the 1070s. It has held Anne Boleyn, the princes in the Tower, and, still, the Crown Jewels.

    Look for: Look for the ravens. Legend says the kingdom will fall if they ever leave, so at least six are kept here.

  • Trafalgar Square

    Square · 1844

    Laid out in the 1840s to remember the Battle of Trafalgar. The fourth plinth is reserved for rotating contemporary sculpture.

    Look for: Edwin Landseer’s four bronze lions guard the base of Nelson’s Column.

  • Westminster Abbey

    Church · 1269

    Edward the Confessor rebuilt a Benedictine abbey here, and every monarch since 1066 has been crowned in it. Poets’ Corner fills the south transept.

    Look for: Just inside the west door, the Grave of the Unknown Warrior is the one tomb in the floor that nobody walks on.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in London and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your London passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
